blocks.text: **Merge sort** is divide and conquer: split the array in half, sort each half (the same way, recursively), and then **merge** the two sorted halves into one. Splitting continues until each piece has one value — and one value is always sorted.

blocks.alt: Merge sort on 38, 27, 43, 3. The array splits into 38, 27 and 43, 3, and again into four single values. Then pairs merge: 38 and 27 become 27, 38; 43 and 3 become 3, 43. Finally 27, 38 and 3, 43 merge into 3, 27, 38, 43.

items: If the array has 0 or 1 values, it's sorted — return it.
Split it into a left half and a right half, and sort each half with merge sort.
**Merge** the two sorted halves: look at the front value of each, move the smaller one to the output, and repeat. When one half runs out, copy the rest of the other.

blocks.text: Merging is the heart of it, and it's fast because both halves are already sorted: the smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of them, so each step is one comparison.

blocks.caption: The array is split down to single values, then merged back up — each merge takes the smaller front value.

blocks.code:
def merge_sort(nums):
    if len(nums) <= 1:
        return nums                       # one value is already sorted
    mid = len(nums) // 2
    left = merge_sort(nums[:mid])         # sort each half...
    right = merge_sort(nums[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)             # ...then merge them


def merge(left, right):
    out = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:           # <= keeps equal values in order: stable
            out.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

blocks.text: Halving n repeatedly reaches 1 after about **log₂ n** levels, and at every level the merges together touch all **n** values once. So merge sort is **O(n log n)** — in the best, average and worst case alike; its running time doesn't depend on the input's order. The merged arrays need **O(n)** extra space (plus O(log n) for the recursion).

blocks.alt: Best, average and worst: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Stable** — on a tie the merge takes from the left half first (`<=`), so equal values keep their order.
**Not in-place** — it needs O(n) extra memory for merging.
**Predictable** — never worse than O(n log n), unlike quick sort.
**Great for linked lists** — splitting and merging only relink nodes, so no extra array is needed (see Sort List).

blocks.text: When you need a **guaranteed** O(n log n), a **stable** sort, or you're sorting a **linked list** or data too big for memory (merging sorted chunks from disk is external sorting). Python's and Java's object sort, Timsort, is a merge sort that also detects already-sorted runs.
The merge step is a pattern of its own: merging sorted lists, counting inversions and Reverse Pairs all reuse it — they're in the last chapter of this course.

items: **Split** in half, **sort** each half recursively, **merge** the sorted halves.
**O(n log n)** in every case, **O(n)** extra space, **stable**.
The merge — repeatedly take the smaller front value — is reused by many interview questions.
